record.paper_title: Reusing Space: Techniques and Open Problems
record.original_question: Can one prove a catalytic analogue of Savitch’s theorem by showing that every nondeterministic catalytic computation using work space s and catalytic space c can be simulated deterministically in catalytic space (s^2, c^2), that is, CNSPACE(s, c) ⊆ CSPACE(s^2, c^2)?

evidence.quote: Problem 23. Prove CNSPACE(s, c) ⊆ CSPACE(s2, c2).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A catalytic Turing machine is a multitape Turing machine equipped with three tapes: a read-only input tape, a read/write work tape, and a read/write catalytic (auxiliary) tape. At the start of the computation, the catalytic tape is initialized with an arbitrary string w ∈ {0,1}^c (the "catalytic content"). During the computation the machine may freely modify both the work tape and the catalytic tape, but it is required that, on every accepting and rejecting computation path and for every initial content w of the catalytic tape, the catalytic tape returns to its original content w at the end of the computation. The work tape uses space at most s = s(n) and the catalytic tape uses space at most c = c(n), where n is the length of the input.

A deterministic catalytic computation must satisfy the above restoration condition on its unique computation path. A nondeterministic catalytic computation is allowed to have a nondeterministic transition function; it accepts an input x if there exists at least one computation path that accepts, and the catalytic-tape restoration condition must hold along every computation path (accepting or rejecting) and for every initial catalytic content.

Define:
- CSPACE(s, c) = the class of languages decided by deterministic catalytic Turing machines using O(s) work space and O(c) catalytic space.
- CNSPACE(s, c) = the class of languages decided by nondeterministic catalytic Turing machines using O(s) work space and O(c) catalytic space.

Problem. Prove or disprove that for all space bounds s = s(n) ≥ log n and c = c(n) ≥ s(n),
    CNSPACE(s, c) ⊆ CSPACE(s^2, c^2).
That is, establish a catalytic analogue of Savitch's theorem showing that every nondeterministic catalytic computation using work space s and catalytic space c can be simulated by a deterministic catalytic computation using work space O(s^2) and catalytic space O(c^2).
artifact.status_search_result: A simulation of the form CNSPACE[s,c] ⊆ CSPACE[O(s^2), O(c)] is known from work of Buhrman, Koucký, Loff, and Speelman on non-determinism and hierarchy in catalytic space (STACS 2016 / TOCS 2017), but with the catalytic tape size preserved (not squared). The specific statement CNSPACE(s,c) ⊆ CSPACE(s^2, c^2) as a full catalytic analogue of Savitch's theorem appears to remain open; recent work on collapsing catalytic classes (2025) does not resolve it.

status_evidence.title: Catalytic Space: Non-determinism and Hierarchy
status_evidence.snippet: CNSPACE[s, c] ⊆ CSPACE[O(s^2), O(c)], showing how nondeterministic catalytic space can be simulated with deterministic catalytic space using a quadratic increase in work space.
status_evidence.claim: A partial catalytic Savitch-type result is known with quadratic work-space blowup but no blowup of the catalytic tape.

status_evidence.title: Collapsing Catalytic Classes
status_evidence.snippet: This paper investigates catalytic space complexity but focuses on collapsing different catalytic classes; the desired quadratic blowup for converting nondeterministic catalytic space to deterministic catalytic space remains an unresolved question.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work does not establish CNSPACE(s,c) ⊆ CSPACE(s^2, c^2) and the problem appears open.
